query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An adaptive surface coating applied to CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy can form a self-adaptive lubricious oxide (e.g., a spinel phase) during high-temperature sliding (up to 800 °C) while maintaining a robust low-friction metallic interface at room temperature, thereby reducing both friction and wear across the entire temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: Monolithic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix with intrinsic sliding tribological behavior.
generation.intervention: Apply an adaptive surface coating via physical vapor deposition that is engineered to transition from a metallic state at low temperatures to a lubricious oxide (spinel phase) at high temperatures.
generation.conditions: Sliding tests under variable loads and environmental conditions over a temperature range from room temperature (~25 °C) to 800 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: The adaptive coating that forms a continuous lubricious oxide layer at high temperatures while retaining a metallic low-friction interface at room temperature.
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures, the coating remains metallic to provide low friction, whereas at elevated temperatures, it oxidizes in a controlled manner to form a lubricious spinel phase that minimizes friction and wear. This temperature-dependent transformation decouples the tribological requirements at low and high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the pristine CoCrFeNi alloy, the coated alloy will exhibit a significantly lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate across the entire temperature range. Specifically, friction and wear improvements should be evident at both room temperature (due to the metallic interface) and at high temperatures (due to the formation of the lubricious oxide layer).
generation.baseline: Unmodified CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy that typically shows increasing friction and wear at elevated temperatures due to lattice disorder and uncontrolled surface oxidation.
generation.boundary: Effective under sliding conditions with moderate loads and in oxidizing environments from room temperature to 800 °C. The intervention may be less effective under extreme loads, highly reducing environments, or if thermal cycling leads to coating delamination.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in friction coefficient and wear rate remain uncertain, as do long-term adhesion and stability of the adaptive coating under cyclic thermal and mechanical stresses.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy samples: one with the adaptive surface coating applied via physical vapor deposition and one as an unmodified control. Subject both sets to sliding tribological tests under identical conditions across the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere. Monitor the surfaces using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to assess the formation of the lubricious oxide layer. Measure the coefficient of friction continuously and determine the wear rate via weight loss and surface profilometry.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) across temperature range
Wear rate (weight loss and surface profilometry)
Surface chemical composition and oxide layer formation (XPS, SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the coated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in both reduced friction and lower wear rate compared to the unmodified samples across the full temperature range, or if the predicted self-adaptive oxide (spinel) layer does not form at elevated temperatures as confirmed by surface analysis.

In this study, the wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy coating was systematically analyzed by the molecular dynamics method. FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy was used as a coating material to adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix. The friction and nanoindentation simulation of this coating material were carried out by controlling the ambient temperature. The influence of temperature on its friction properties was analyzed on five aspects: lattice structure, dislocation evolution, friction coefficient, hardness, and elastic modulus. At 300 K and 600 K, the ordered lattice structure of the high entropy alloy coating material is basically the same, and thus its hardness is basically the same. The appearance of high entropy alloys breaks the traditional design concept of alloys based on mixing enthalpy and opens up a broad space for composition design for the research and development of new materials. The comprehensive effect of the mixing of various main elements endows the high entropy alloy with high entropy effect in thermodynamics, lattice distortion effect in structure, hysteresis diffusion effect in dynamics, and “cocktail” effect in performance [ [1] , [2] ]. The principle of multi-principal element design based on these four effects results in the high entropy alloy showing many unique properties beyond the traditional alloy. These characteristics cover excellent corrosion resistance [ [3] ], wear resistance [ [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] ], excellent fatigue strength, and yield strength under various temperature conditions [ [10] , [11] ], high hardness [ [12] ], excellent microstructure stability and thermal stability [ [13] , [14] ], and excellent high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [15] ]. The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. As a result, precipitation strengthening should be considered in developing HEAs for high temperature applications. The physical metallurgy of superalloys [9] have been employed to design HEAs by utilization of significant volume fractions of stable and coherent L1 2 γ′ to provide high temperature strength, e.g., Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 HEA was designed to contain 46 vol% of γ′ precipitates [10] , and its tensile strength could surpass those of Inconel 617 and All

Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

decision.trend: Early work in high‐entropy alloys and related self‐lubricating systems has shown that modifying the material—either by adding elements like Ti to form multiphase microstructures that generate lubricious, high‐temperature oxide (spinel) interfaces or by tailoring processing routes to control phase formation—can reduce friction at high temperatures. For example, PMC7515071 demonstrated that introducing Ti into an AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 system promoted oxide formation that lowered the coefficient of friction at elevated temperatures, while studies on SLM‐produced high-entropy alloys (PMC7229066) showed that microstructural design can help maintain mechanical integrity across a range of temperatures. However, many of these interventions optimize performance only at one end of the temperature spectrum or inadvertently degrade room-temperature performance.
decision.unsolved: The remaining challenge is to design one intervention for a CoCrFeNi alloy that can consistently achieve low friction and wear over the entire wide temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C) under varying load and environmental conditions. In other words, an approach is needed that decouples high-temperature lubricity from low-temperature impact without compromising the inherent properties of the alloy.
decision.lever: Develop an adaptive surface coating (e.g., using physical vapor deposition) that is engineered to form a continuous, self-adaptive lubricious oxide (such as a spinel phase) at high temperatures while retaining a robust, low-friction metallic interface at room temperature.
decision.why: This approach directly follows the observed trend: previous systems have leveraged controlled oxide formation to achieve low friction at elevated temperatures (as seen in self-lubricating material systems and in PMC7515071) but have not yet optimized the full temperature range in CoCrFeNi alloys. Surface/interface engineering permits independent control of the tribological surface without altering the bulk material, addressing the requirement to maintain performance under varying operational conditions.
